newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Boutros-Ghali's future hovers over assembly session.
newsitem.headline: Boutros-Ghali's future hovers over assembly session.

text.p: Like Banquo's ghost, Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali's future hovers over the 51st General Assembly session, where few countries were expected to mention publicly the subject of his re-election.

But unlike the specter in Shakespeare's "Macbeth," the U.N. secretary-general is invited to the procedings, defying the United States by declaring his intention to seek another five years when his current term expires in December.

With kings, presidents, prime ministers and foreign ministers gathering at the United Nations for the next three weeks, beginning on Monday, no one knows who will lead the world body next year or what the nearly bankrupt organisation is supposed to do.

For Washington, how the United Nations operates, rather than what its tasks are, is foremost, beginning with the search for a new secretary-general who would concentrate on restructuring the world body.

"What we want to do now is to have countries begin to look seriously at alternative candidates ... in October to have the Security Council set up a timetable and a process both for receiving nominations, considering them and eventually voting," Princeton Lyman, the U.S. assistant secretary of state for international organisations, said on Friday.

But so far no formal process has begun and none is expected until after the Nov. 5 U.S. presidential election. Most delegates believe opposition to Boutros-Ghali is politically motivated, and the council last month rebuffed efforts by U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright even to discuss the issue.
According to Russia's U.N. ambassador, Sergei Lavrov, the majority of the 15-seat council believes "November is the good time to start discussion of the substance of the issue."

But Albright, who announced in December that Boutros-Ghali must go, said flatly that "the administration will not change its mind, if re-elected. We are prepared to use our veto." She said the United States wanted first and foremost an administrator rather than a statesman, one "who is not dragged into (reform) kicking and screaming."

To many analysts, Albright apparently believes Congress will never agree to pay the $1.6 billion in arrears the United States owes to the United Nations without some radical change, such as a new secretary-general.

Conversely, with Congress' refusal to pay the huge debt crippling the world body, American authority has been so undercut that other U.N. members are ready to turn down many initiatives suggested by Washington.

China, which also has veto power, has given notice that if Boutros-Ghali, an Egyptian, is not re-elected it would support another candidate from Africa, and if that fails a candidate from another developing nation.

By this logic, all women mentioned for the job -- Irish President Mary Robinson, Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland and U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata of Japan -- would be excluded. The exception might be Philippine Sen. Leticia Ramos Shahani, who has declared her candidacy.

Among the African candidates mentioned most frequently are Kofi Annan of Ghana, the U.N. undersecretary-general for peacekeeping, and Salim A. Salim, chairman of the Organisation of African Unity. In addition, Hamid Algabid of Niger, the head of the Islamic Conference, has announced his candidacy.

Deciding who should lead the organisation will not resolve the issue of where its focus should be. Peacekeeping, once the centre of its activities, has dwindled to 25,000 soldiers from more than 70,000 two years ago.

Boutros-Ghali himself is philosophical about the direction of the United Nations. "It took around 10 years to agree about the rules of the Cold War, to manage the Cold War and the institutions to apply those rules," he said, mentioning the creation of NATO in 1949 and the Warsaw Pact in 1955.

"In our case, we are still at the beginning and the member states don't know what role they want from the United Nations," he told Reuters last week. "Now we are living in a crisis of the United Nations -- its ups and downs."
